name: Ingrid Solberg
headline: 34, owner of a smoked-fish company, Bergen
title: Sunday Fjord Invitation
situation: On a bright Sunday morning, Ingrid is at the loft reviewing brine charts when her retired neighbor, Lars, knocks on the door. He tells her that a few people from the dock are taking his old boat out to fish along the fjord, a traditional excursion she remembers from her childhood. He offers her a spare rod and a spot onboard. Ingrid knows that joining would mean losing a few hours of weekend work on her competition prep, but it also offers a rare chance to reconnect with the pastime her father loved and the local customs she grew up with.

context.relationship_profiles:
Lars is a retired neighbor who once crewed with her father; he sends weather jokes each week and has not pushed when she misses his dock gatherings.
Her father's illness defines their fragile daily rhythm; she audits his caregivers and visits every afternoon, carrying quiet guilt about selling his boat.
context.tendencies:
When weekend invitations overlap with production prep, she consistently declines; she has skipped three dock gatherings this season.
Sunday follows a fixed order: smokehouse walk, father visit, then anything else.
She contributes to dugnad with supplies rather than time, protecting her strategy.
context.current_state:
She has been up since 4 AM testing brine and reviewing Week 14 pricing; eyes tired, hands steady.
Sunday's smokehouse walk is still pending, and the afternoon father visit is scheduled, leaving only the morning open.
No urgent quality or payroll issue is pending; the loft is quiet, smelling of fresh smoke.
context.immediate_memories:
Lars's old boat evokes summer Sundays on her father's fjord cruiser, coiling rope and listening to men argue over herring runs.
The tarred rope smell in the loft is her childhood cue, but today it brings her father's hands on the tiller before the dementia.
context.reflective_memories:
She has not been on the fjord since selling her father's boat for the loft; only the engine bolt on the windowsill remains.
Her grandmother called the fjord 'the first ledger,' a phrase Ingrid still repeats when she reads tides.
Her father said a Sunday on the water was fuel, not lost work, though she has long counted hours differently.
